Dear Reviewer B4H5,

Thank you for your detailed feedback on our paper. Below, we respond to each of your comments and explain the changes we have made accordingly. 

**On the choice of the $\ell_1$​-norm**

First and foremost, we would like to emphasize that our empirical observations are not specific to the $\ell_1$​-norm of the parameters (cf. the last sentence of (i) of our contribution statement). As shown in Appendix H.9, we also compare results for other norms, and the qualitative trends remain consistent. Our goal is to understand the effect of norm-based regularization rather than a specific choice of norm. Our systematic experimental results reveal consistent trade-offs across all settings, suggesting that even independent of theoretical motivation, the behavior of the $\ell_1$-norm of the parameters remains a meaningful and informative quantity to analyze. 

**On the theoretical study:**

The reviewer is right that we insufficiently distinguished between the parameter vector $\mathbf w_\star$ and the end-to-end solution $\mathbf w_\star^{\odot 2}$ in Section 3. This leads to confusion and incorrect statements in in-text explanations. The confusion is further amplified by our decision to plot the $\ell_1$-norm of the parameters in the realistic set-ups, instead of the more generic $\ell_2$-norm. \
We made the distinction more clear in the revised version. First, when discussing our empirical results, we speak of norm bias instead of $\ell_1$-norm bias. Second, we correct our statement in Section 3: for small learning rates $\mathbf w_\star$ will have minimal $\ell_2$-norm. Since our results on realistic networks show the same qualitative trade-offs when replacing the $\ell_1$- with the $\ell_2$-norm of the parameters, this even strengthens the link between the empirical studies and our simplified toy model.
To us it is very surprising that the observed trade-off seems to be similar for different choices of norm (see Section H.9 and I.8.1). At the moment, we do not have a satisfactory explanation for this.

**On the scope of our theory for diagonal networks.**

In the revised version of Section 3, we expanded our analysis of the generalization error and now show that the toy model reproduces the phenomena observed empirically in realistic training. This includes the norm/sharpness trade-off and the U-shaped generalization error. The added material compares GD to three idealized algorithms with different risk (norm-minimizer, sharpness-minimizer, and risk minimizer), and shows which of these algorithms GD approximates depending on the learning rate. In particular, the GD limit is often close to a KKT point of a sharpness-restricted risk minimization on the solution manifold (see Figure 15 and Lemma E.1).

**On the y-axis of Figure 2.**

Yes, as indicated by the label, the $y$-axis of Figure 2 (and all other figures where we report the $\ell_1$-norm) represents the $\ell_1$-norm of the model parameters.

**On the $\ell_1$-norm increase during EoS.**

You asked whether the observed increase in the $\ell_1$-norm could be an artifact of the oscillations, rather than indicating that the trajectory visits regions of higher norm. In Figure 13 (Figure 12 of the original submission), we show the temporal trajectories of the relevant quantities. As you can see, while the sharpness oscillates, the $\ell_1$-norm remains largely monotonically increasing and does not oscillate. This indicates that the oscillations occur within regions of similar norm, and therefore the observed $\ell_1$-norm increase reflects that the trajectory indeed moves toward regions of higher norm, rather than being an effect of oscillatory dynamics. \
Averaging the weights norms of the final last steps therefore would not lead to a qualitative change of the $\ell_1$-norm increase. Decaying the learning rate before reaching the edge of stability will likely lead to a norm consistent with the flow-aligned regime.


We would like to thank you again for your thoughtful critique, especially raising the valid point of the $\ell_1$-norm of the end-to-end classifier versus the weights. We hope our explanations and adjustments of the paper resolve your concerns. In this case, we would greatly appreciate it if you reconsider your scoring. Should you have any remaining questions or doubts, please let us know, we would be happy to provide further clarifications.

*Part 1 of 2*

Dear Reviewer 2XC6,

We would like to thank you for your thoughtful review and helpful and detailed remarks on how to improve the work. We appreciate you liked our presentation and find the contribution interesting to the community. Below, we respond to your comments and questions. 

**On expanding the theory.**

We have incorporated your suggestion that generalization of the toy model should already be discussed in the main paper and moved relevant parts to Section 3. Additionally, we have extended our analysis. The added material compares GD to three idealized algorithms with different risk (norm-minimizer, sharpness-minimizer, and risk minimizer), and shows which of these algorithms GD approximates depending on the learning rate. In particular, the GD limit is often close to a KKT point of a sharpness-restricted risk minimization on the solution manifold (see Figure 15 and Lemma E.1).

We furthermore understand the reviewer’s concern about the validity of our strongly simplified training set-up with a single data point. We agree that in this case empirical and true risk are not close to each other such that it is impossible to infer good generalization from minimizing the empirical risk. However, we highlight that despite its simplicity, our toy model is able to reproduce core features of our general experiments such as norm and sharpness curves exhibiting increasing and decreasing behavior with sharp phase transitions, and a U-shaped curve over the test error, see our newly added material in Section 3 (in particular updated Figures 4 and 14). We do not think that this is purely coincidental, and thus believe that the present analysis provides a formal argument for the trade-off we observe empirically. We also believe that an extension of our analysis to several data points could be done in principle (likely yielding a similar conclusion, i.e. the minimizers differ and the characteristic curves of norm, sharpness and generalization are reproduced). In this case, the solution manifold is an intersection of several ellipsoids and the empirical risk is a reasonable approximation of the true risk. However, as a full theoretical analysis of the observed phenomenon in this setting is technically challenging and beyond the scope of the present paper, we see this as interesting future work.

**On your questions regarding Figure 1:**

*Question 1:*

> Could the authors comment on the form of the critical step size $\eta_c$? Why is $\eta_c$ related to the maximal sharpness of the GF solutions? This paper [1] might be relevant.\
\
 [1] Kreisler, Itai, et al. "Gradient descent monotonically decreases the sharpness of gradient flow solutions in scalar networks and beyond." International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR, 2023.

Theorem B.2 shows that GD can almost surely converge only to solutions with sharpness below $2/\eta$. For MSE loss, the maximal sharpness of the GF solution typically occurs towards the end of training. Hence, GD cannot almost surely converge to the GF solution once the step size exceeds $\eta_c$. In contrast, for CE loss, the sharpness typically decreases again after a phase of oscillations around $2/\eta$; however, by that point, the GF sharpness is already below this threshold, indicating that the trajectories have already diverged. It is also worth noting that the instability during the EoS regime leads to non-monotonic loss behavior, whereas prior to this regime, the loss decreases monotonically according to the descent lemma (Equation (2) in our introduction). We therefore interpret step sizes beyond $\eta_c$ as explicitly preventing GD from following the GF trajectory at the time when the sharpness reaches its maximum if the two trajectories remained close up to that point (although in practice, they may diverge earlier).

Regarding the sharpness of the GF solution introduced in [1], this quantity requires restarting GF during training. In our analysis, however, we focus only on the final point reached by GD. If we were to restart GF at some intermediate step for learning rates within the flow-aligned regime, we would expect the restarted GF solution to reproduce similar values as the original GD. Note that for such learning rates, GD does not enter the EoS regime, so this behavior does not contradict the findings of [1]. In contrast, for learning rates beyond $\eta_c$, we would indeed expect the GFS sharpness to decrease if GF were restarted from an intermediate GD iterate during EoS. We also added this reference to our literature review on EoS.

*Please also see Part 2 for our answer to the other questions.*

Dear Reviewer 2XC6,

Thank you very much for replying. We will start our answer with your main concern, and then reply to your remaining questions/comments.

> This is insufficient for supporting the main claim "generalization cannot be explained by a single bias".

The goal of our theory is to provide concrete counterexamples to the claims (1) the flattest minimum always generalizes best, and (2) the smallest-norm solution always generalizes best. This is also what we stated in our Contribution (iii): \
 *“Serving as a basic counterexample in which single biases do not generalize optimally, this supports our conjecture that the generalization behavior of neural networks can not be explained by a single implicit bias of GD.”* \
Concretely, we show that:

* in the setting of Section 3 we have that the risk of the norm minimizer is smaller than the risk of the sharpness minimizer on the solution manifold 
* whereas in the setting of section F we obtain the opposite relation, i.e. the risk of the norm minimizer is *larger* than the risk of the sharpness minimizer.

As we wrote in our initial reply, we agree the empirical risk and true risk can be far from each other. Our intention is not to fully characterize the generalization of the toy model. 

> If I understand correctly, the primary update in Section 3 is Figure 4 [...].

Your summary of Figure 4 is correct. In particular, we present the empirical results on the toy model in comparison to the theoretical prediction to highlight that they agree.

In addition to that, we have also revised Lemma E.1 to include new material, most importantly the characterization of the KKT points of the risk minimization under the sharpness constraint $2/\eta$ (Lemma B.2). Building on this, we expanded our discussion of the three idealized algorithms with different risk (norm-minimizer, sharpness-minimizer, and risk minimizer) and moved them to Section 3.

>  My questions are, what is the training data used in Figure 4, and, do those observations hold for general training data?

> For the 2D case $w=(w_1,w_2)$, the solution set is: $w_{1}^2 x_{0,1} + w_{2}^2 x_{0,2} = y_0$. Under a random $(x_0,y_0)$, the geometry of this set can have a very high variation, e.g., ellipsoid, hyperbola, or two straight lines.

When introducing the risk model, we condition the data distribution to have both coordinates of $x_0$ and $y_0$ positive which makes the solution set an ellipse. Positive features naturally arise when modelling physical quantities. The exemplary data point used in the shown experiments is $x_0 = (0.5, 3), y_0 = 1$. 

We would like to emphasize that the main goal of the theory is not to give a rigorous analysis of the phenomenon in full generality, but to help interpret the empirical observation and demonstrate the underlying principle. 

We hope this clarifies the intention behind the theory and the scope of our claims.
Please let us know if there remain aspects we can clarify further.

Dear Reviewer nZYx,

We thank you for your encouraging review and are glad you found our work sound and the comprehensive experiments convincing. 

Implicit bias of gradient descent and its variants is a common explanation for why models generalize well despite being heavily overparameterized and capable of memorizing the dataset. Much of the existing theory studies this effect in simplified or toy settings where the analysis is tractable. At the same time, several regularization techniques widely used in practice are grounded in these theoretical findings: For example, weight decay corresponds to norm regularization, and SAM is linked to sharpness regularization.
 
Our systematic experiments reveal a consistent trade-off between low sharpness and low parameter norm across varying core training components, demonstrating that these commonly assumed “beneficial biases” cannot, in general, be achieved simultaneously. By clarifying the limitations of existing intuitions, we aim to guide both theory and practice toward more reliable, theoretically grounded optimization strategies in deep learning. At the same time, our work is foundational in nature and does not have an immediate practical consequence. \
We agree that the learning rate is indeed a well-known and influential hyperparameter in practice; however, we believe that framing learning rate as a mechanism that balances between conflicting biases offers a novel and valuable perspective for both the theoretical and practitioner communities. Our theoretical analysis confirms this interpretation. 


>Maybe it would be interesting to define a new parameterized bias that captures sharpness and -norm at the extremes and then investigate theoretically how generalization can depend on that parameter?

We are not perfectly sure if we understand your suggestion correctly. In case you mean designing an explicit regularizer that interpolates between the low-norm and low-sharpness bias, our newly added material to Section 3 may address that. There, we derive a theoretical U-shaped curve for our simplified model which correctly predicts the generalization error reached by GD as we interpolate between minimal norm and minimal sharpness via tuning the learning rate parameter.


We expanded our Discussion (Section 4) to highlight future directions, including extending the interaction to additional known biases and to more realistic optimizers. This also directly links back to your question on practical relevance.

Thank you again for your thoughtful feedback. If our clarifications address your concerns, we would greatly appreciate it if you would consider raising the score. We are happy to provide any further explanation if needed.

*Part 2 of 2*

*Question 2:*

>The final norm and final sharpness simultaneously exhibit a sharp transition at $\eta=\eta_c$ . Could the authors provide intuition for the emergence of such a sharp transition?

We don’t have a good explanation why the phase transition is so sharp. In particular, as we show with the distance from the GF solution (see Section H.10), the trajectories deviate from each other already for learning rates in the flow-aligned regime, despite their limits still matching in sharpness and norm values. We also mention that the $\ell_1$-norm increase is not always occurring at $\eta_c$ but sometimes at a larger step size (cf. Figure 16 of the revised version/ Figure 15 of the original submission).

*Question 3:*

>Could the authors explain the trade off between the final norm and the final sharpness?
 
We believe that the increased norm is a consequence of EoS and the fact that in these training setups the sharpness and norm minimizers do not agree. Specifically, while GF would converge to a solution of small norm, the instability of discrete GD updates causes the trajectory to deviate from these low-norm minima. We illustrate this intuition in our diagonal model, where, once the learning rate becomes too large to settle close to the GF optimum, GD oscillates around the minima of zero loss (yellow ellipse) towards flatter regions, usually converging around the first point sufficiently flat to accommodate the step size. We emphasize, however, that this behavior is not universal, i.e. for very large $\eta$, the instability can also catapult the iterates towards other flat minima, not necessarily the closest one to initialization (see Figure 15 of the revised version/ Figure 14 of the original submission).

>Why should we expect a decrease in sharpness corresponds to an increase in the norm?
 
As we show in Proposition 3.2, for the diagonal model, there are no minima of simultaneously low sharpness and low norm. For the empirical study, we cannot give a conclusive answer to the existence of such minima, but our results show that GD does not find any.

> This is in contrast with the scalar factorization case, $L(x,y)=(x^\top y -a)^2$ , where the squared norm of a minimizer is equal to the sharpness (see, e.g., Theorem F.2, [2]).\
\
[2] Yuqing Wang, Minshuo Chen, Tuo Zhao, and Molei Tao. Large Learning Rate Tames Homogeneity: Convergence and Balancing Effect. ICLR 2022



You are right that for the scalar factorization case, the norm and sharpness minimizers agree. As mentioned in our literature review (paragraph on generalization and $\ell_1$-norm) there are examples in the literature where independent biases coincide, for example in (overparameterized) matrix regression the sharpness and nuclear norm ($\ell_1$-norm on the spectrum) minimizers lie close to each other, which provably generalize well in low-rank recovery. The scalar factorization provides another example we were not aware of. In our revised version, we have added the citation [2] you suggested to our literature review.

We hope our revised paper communicates these points about the intuition behind Figure 1 more clearly.

Thank you again for your valuable feedback. If our reply, in particular the expanded theory and the explanations to Figure 1 have resolved your concerns, we would greatly appreciate it if you would consider increasing your score.

summary.value: This paper measures the sharpness and $\ell_1$ norms of neural networks trained by gradient descent with varying learning rates and observes a tradeoff between the $\ell_1$ norm and the sharpness. They investigate the effect of this tradeoff on generalization and theoretically analyze a diagonal linear network to gain insights into this tradeoff.

strengths.value:
- The empirical results are verified in a variety of settings with many additional plots in the Appendix. This includes multiple architectures, datasets, and loss functions. In addition, the empirical setup is extensively detailed in the appendix, which provides strong evidence for the claimed tradeoff between $\ell_1$ norm and sharpness.
- The paper proposes multiple theoretical analyses for understanding the tradeoff between $\ell_1$ norm including an analysis of the diagonal linear net, and generalization analyses under different norms (Appendix E)

weaknesses.value:
- I believe that while the result is correctly stated in Appendix B, the paper mischaracterizes the results of Woodworth et al. throughout the rest of the paper. Their result is that under the model $f_w(x) = w^{\odot 2} \cdot x$, gradient flow with small initialization will converge to the parameter $w$ with minimal $\ell_2$ norm. If one defines the implicit classifier $\beta = w^{\odot 2}$ then this is equivalent to finding $\beta$ of minimal  norm as $\|\beta\|_1 = \|w\|_2^2$. **Woodworth et al. does not claim the weights $w$ will have minimal $\ell_1$ norm.**
- As far as I am aware, there is no mechanism for $\ell_1$ regularization in general neural networks (outside of the linear nets with small initialization), and for linear networks this implicit bias is usually stated for the implicit end-to-end linear classifier, not for the weights themselves. This calls into question the empirical results on realistic neural networks which appear to measure the $\ell_1$ norm of the parameters themselves.
- For the diagonal linear network, the paper only argues that the minimal $\ell_1$ norm solution is inconsistent with the edge of stability at large learning rates and does not actually characterize the solutions that gradient descent converges to.

questions.value:
- In Figure 2, is the quantity on the $y$ axis the $L^1$ norm of the parameters $\|\theta\|_1$? If so, what evidence is there for $\ell_1$ weight norm as an implicit bias of gradient descent?
- Because the dynamics of gradient descent are highly oscillatory at the edge of stability, it seems possible that the increase in the $\ell_1$ norm at the edge of stability could be due to the oscillations, and not necessarily because gradient descent visits regions of higher $\ell_1$ norm. How does the $\ell_1$ norm change if you average the weights over a few steps before computing the norm? Or decay the learning rate and then compute the norm before it reaches the edge of stability at the new learning rate?

summary.value: The paper's core claim is as follows -- As the learning rate increases past a critical value, full-batch GD exhibits a trade-off between (i) low parameter norm (GF/small-step implicit bias) and (ii) low sharpness (EoS/large-step implicit bias), and neither bias alone reliably explains best generalization. The paper performs as a systematic sweep showing a sharp regime change at a critical learning rate and an apparent norm <--> sharpness tradeoff across many variants (architectures, norms, losses, etc.). The paper also provides a toy diagonal-network analysis where norm-minimizers and sharpness-minimizers differ, and (in the toy) intermediate learning rates can be closer to a “best generalization” solution than either extreme.

reviewer_concerns.value:
Reviewer B4H5

(1) Mischaracterization of Woodworth et al.: implicit bias is about the end-to-end predictor, not “weights have min norm.” -- authors acknowledge and correct it. 

(2) Empirics measure parameter norm—what justifies that as “implicit bias” in realistic nets? -- The authors broaden framing to “norm bias” across norms, and add per-layer norms / intrinsic-time plots, but the deeper conceptual leap—why parameter norm should be viewed as the bias relevant to generalization in real nets is still not fully answered.

(3) Diagonal model: they didn’t characterize where GD converges at large LR. -- authors add material computing constrained KKT points / show GD converges to them; reviewer calls this “nice additions” that “strengthen the section.”

(4) Norm increase might be an artifact of oscillations; asked for averaging/decay checks. -- Authors point to temporal plots showing sharpness oscillates but norm is “largely monotonically increasing and does not oscillate,” arguing oscillations are not driving norm growth.


Reviewer 2XC6

(1) Concerns about theory, concerned about Appendix E is single-sample and not convincing for “generalization can’t be explained by a single bias.” 
(2) Unclear about how \eta_c relates to GF sharpness
(3) After rebuttal: still skeptical—Figure 4 depends on a specific training datum; with one sample the solution set varies a lot; empirical comparisons aren’t enough to support the headline claim. 

Concerns largely unaddressed, the paper can improve a lot by resolving these.

Reviewer F2HG
(1) Scale-invariance of the sharpness meeasure, 
(2) Underexplored regularization (weight decay, batch norm)
Concerns were addressed by the authors and the reviewer acknowledged, no indication of score increase. 

The core theory-as-support-for-generalization story remains weak: multiple reviewers have expressed concerns that were not resolved during the rebuttal.

*Part 1 of 2* 

Dear reviewer B4H5,

Thank you very much for your prompt reply and also for the increased score! We would like to comment on the newly raised points and hopefully resolve your remaining concerns: 

**Studying arbitrary norms** 

To further emphasize independence of our results from the choice of norm, we now plot different norms in Figures 1 – 3. We also further deemphasize the $\ell_1$-norm in the contribution and in Section 2. Rather than switching the role of the $\ell_1$- and $\ell_2$-norm, the revised version of Section 2 no longer centers on one main norm, but on the norm bias more broadly general. 

Following your suggestion, we have plotted the temporal evolution in intrinsic time and updated Figure 13 accordingly. For the norm, the behaviour is exactly as you expected: larger learning rates grow faster. The training times, however, do not align perfectly across learning rates. We discuss this in *Appendix H.8* and in *Appendix I.8.2* where we show the “curve length”, i.e. $\eta \cdot$ #iterations, when varying the learning rate. The general tendency is that the curve length increases with the learning rate, in other words, larger learning rates tend to train slower in intrinsic time. However, the relationship is not strictly monotone as you can see in the plots in Section I.8.2. and also in the setup in the updated Figure 13 of the temporal evolution.

Our per-layer norm analysis confirms that the layer norms show an increasing trend over the learning rate. As one might expect, the increase in layer norm is relative to the number of parameters of the layer. We added respective experiments to Section H.12. 
 
**Updated Section 3**

> My understanding is that the main updates are Figure 15 and Lemma E.1. 

In addition to the changes mentioned by you, we have updated the second half of Section 3 in the main text, including the new Figure 4d showing the U-shaped generalization curve. 

> To make sure I'm understanding correctly, the paper doesn't provide any mechanistic explanation for why you converge to these points, correct?  
> Is the intuition that you should converge to some stable interpolator, and it seems reasonable to hope that it's the min norm stable interpolator as a way of reconciling the two implicit biases? 

Yes indeed, this is the intuition we also gained, however we do not have a formal proof for this proximity.

> For learning rates (e)-(k), the dynamics cleanly converge to a KKT point but I can't tell what happens for learning rate (l) since the dynamics seem to stop at an arbitrary point on $\mathcal{M}$. Do the dynamics just diverge?

For the learning rate shown in 15(l), the dynamics become highly unstable. However, the dynamics do converge (to that point on the solution manifold where the trajectory line ends, between the purple and black circle). When we examine the intrinsic time required to reach a certain training loss, we note that it takes significantly longer ($2.2\times$ more) than the next smaller learning rate shown in 15(k). Further, all learning rates beyond $\eta = 0.333$ on the equally spaced grid diverge. 

This also shows that the intuition about the “min norm stable interpolator” holds only up to a certain level of stability; Once the dynamics become too unstable, we can no longer make meaningful statements about the limit of GD. Note that even for smaller learning rates (Figures 15(i) and 15(j)), GD does not converge to the closest stable interpolator in terms of distance to initialization, although the found solution is still min-norm under the sharpness constraints (we initialize in the first quadrant, i.e., all positive entries).

> This is outside the scope of this work, but I'm curious how well the GD dynamics follow projected gradient flow constrained to the set   (the "central flow" in [1]). If they do, it may be possible to generalize the proof technique in Woodworth et al. to argue that you should converge to one of the KKT points in Lemma E.1

Due to the "discontinuities" just discussed (e.g., in Figure 15 (h) versus 15 (i) the GD limit differs), it might be hard to study unstable GD for very large learning rates also with projected gradient descent. Nevertheless we can imagine that an analysis for moderately large step sizes is approachable via this.

*Please also see Part 2 for the continuation of our answer.*

Dear AC, 

Given the changes to the review-process, we would like to summarize the state of the discussion for you:

**Reviewer B4H5 -  initial score: 2, raised to 4, positive trend**

* Stated the experiments provide *”strong evidence for the claimed tradeoff”*.
* Identified a valid mistake, which we corrected: that for the diagonal network the end-to-end classifier is biased towards a low $\ell_1$-norm, but weights biased toward low $\ell_2$-norm. The reviewer acknowledged the correction with an increased score (4).
* Their second critique that we do not *”actually characterize the solutions that gradient descent converges to”* was addressed by the new material in Section 3. They wrote *“computation of the constrained KKT points and the empirical observation that GD does indeed converge to these points are nice additions and definitely strengthen the section.”*
* We also ran additional experiments (batch normalization, per-layer-norm analysis) and carefully answered the remaining questions of their initial reply. The reviewer did not have the opportunity to reply again before the abrupt stop, but the development of our discussion was clearly positive.

**Reviewer bSo1 - initial score: 0, we respectfully request exclusion**

* Multiple statements were factually incorrect (e.g., claims about missing citations, MNIST lacking EoS dynamics), despite highest reviewer confidence (5).
* We documented these issues in detail paragraph-per-paragraph. The reviewer did not engage further or correct them. 
* Given this poor-quality review, we respectfully request excluding this review from the final decision.

**Reviewer nZYx - initial score: 4, no reply**

* Positive on soundness, clarity, and empirical breadth: the paper *“does a very good job of highlighting the different bias behaviors of GD depending on the learning rate“*. They requested *“pointing out either concrete conclusions/guidance for practitioners and/or open problems that if addressed successfully in future work would have significant impact.”*
* In the revision, we expanded the Discussion, clarified practitioner relevance, and strengthened Section 3’s interpretation of the U-shaped generalization curve. The reviewer has not replied before the cut.

**Reviewer 2XC6 - initial score: 6**

* Praised *“I find the main message and the experiments valuable to the community”*.
* Had questions on the interpretation of Figure 1, which we answered in detail with no follow-up question. We also incorporated elements of these explanations into the revised version to improve clarity. 
* Their main critique was on the generalization model, that the true and empirical risk don’t have to be close. We fully agree that it is not sufficient to fully characterize generalization of the toy model, but emphasize that we intend to provide a counterexample that single biases do not generalize optimally. Also, the model displays the core characteristics of our larger scale experiments. For their other remarks, we believe we have answered them in full, e.g. that the solution set is an ellipsoid under our data assumption. 

**Reviewer F2HG - initial score 6, positive trend**

* Praised the framing (*“furthers the discussion on [...] implicit bias”*) and empirical breadth.
* Requested alternative sharpness measures, batch normalization experiments, other data modalities and additional references. In the first revision, submitted before the reviewer’s last reply, we had already incorporated part of these additions, and the reviewer explicitly acknowledged that these resolved their concerns.
* After that exchange, we added a second set of improvements (other data modalities experiments to H.14, alternative sharpness measures to H.9, batch normalization to H.2) to the revision. We also answered their remaining questions. Due to the abrupt end of the discussion phase, the reviewer did not have the opportunity to respond to these further updates.
* Given the positive trend of the discussion and the substantial additional improvements after their last reply, we believe the reviewer would possibly have increased the score.

Across the engaged reviewers, the discussion was highly constructive and we believe we were able to resolve all substantive concerns. The paper has improved significantly: we expanded Section 3 (new generalization result), emphasized the independence of norm choice, added additional experiments (other data modalities, batch normalization, scale-invariant sharpness measures) and an expanded literature review to the revision. Based on the interactions with the reviewers, we believe that the paper would have experienced several increased scores if the discussion would not have been cut short.

We would be happy to answer any further questions you may have. Thank you for your time and for your effort under the unusual circumstances of ICLR 2026.

Dear reviewers,

We have now uploaded a second revised version to which we added the new experiments. The concrete changes are:

* **H.2 Architecture**: We have included a variation of our CNN architecture with an additional batch normalization layer and updated the text accordingly. The corresponding plot replaces Figure 5c, the original set-up is now shown in Appendix I.

In addition to that, we have made the following modifications based on your feedback to our rebuttal:

* We added the references mentioned during the rebuttal phase to the literature review.
* We made some very minor reformulations in order to stay within the page limit.

If you have any questions or concerns about these updates, please let us know.

Thank you for the detailed responses! I still have some concerns about the theory section. 

If I understand correctly, the primary update in Section 3 is Figure 4, where the authors considered a specific training data, and empirically showed that as $\eta$ increases, the sharpness decreases, the norm increases, and the test error exhibits a U-curve. 

All observations in Figure 4 are made under a specific training data $(x_0,y_0)$. My questions are, what is the training data used in Figure 4, and, do those observations hold for general training data?  

When the training data changes, the solution set changes, and so do the norm-minimizer, sharpness-minimizer, and risk minimizer. With a large sample size, the variation of this change is small and I expect that some meaningful results can be obtained. However, with one single sample, the variation should be very large and I doubt that the observations in Figure 4 persist consistently. For the 2D case $w=(w_1,w_2)$, the solution set is: $w_{1}^2 x_{0,1} + w_{2}^2 x_{0,2} = y_0$. Under a random $(x_0,y_0)$, the geometry of this set can have a very high variation, e.g., ellipsoid, hyperbola, or two straight lines. 

Also, the comparison among the generalization of the norm-minimizer, sharpness-minimizer, and risk minimizer is made only empirically and based on a specific training data, as in Figure 4. This is insufficient for supporting the main claim "generalization cannot be explained by a single bias".

I would like to thank the authors for their response.

My questions have been answered.

I do also like to know the answer to the question by Reviewer 2XC6 about the solution set.

Reviewer bSo1, highlighted a beyond EOS regime result. I do would like to emphasize that the beyond EOS result shows that with higher learning rate can lead to balancing which in turn leads to low norm again. Therefore, the perceived trade off between norm and sharpness happens only between the gradient flow and EOS regime. This should be mentioned in the manuscript and not just as an additional citation as it is now.

* **Section 2 - Conflicting biases:** We now talk about norm bias instead of $\ell_1$-norm bias to emphasize that the results are independent of the studied norm.

We highlight that this includes new material. The added material compares GD to three idealized algorithms with different risk (norm-minimizer, sharpness-minimizer, and risk minimizer), and shows which of these algorithms GD approximates depending on the learning rate. In particular, the GD limit is often close to a KKT point of a sharpness-restricted risk minimization on the solution manifold (see Figure 15 and Lemma E.1). We also update Figure 4 to reflect these results. Secondly, we correct our mistake: the implicit bias of the weights of the diagonal model is toward small $\ell_2$-norm, whereas the bias of the final classifier is toward small $\ell_1$-norm.

*Part 1 of 2*

Dear Reviewer F2HG,

We thank you for your encouraging review.  We appreciate you found our framing novel and the results convincing. Below, we address your comments and questions:

**On the literature on diagonal networks**

> Based on these two works ([1,2]), would this suggest that the L1 bias is preferred at all times? 

Although an $\ell_1$-norm bias is desirable in many applications because it promotes sparsity, this does not imply that it is always preferred, i.e. different settings may favor other forms of regularization.
We would also like to point out a correction to our theoretical discussion: the $\ell_1$-norm bias holds for the end-to-end classifier, not for the weights (see also our reply to Reviewer B4H5). We corrected this in the revised version. For the diagonal model, the weights are instead biased toward small $\ell_2$-norm. 
Even in studies of the end-to-end classifier in the diagonal case, the implicit bias or regularization is typically more complex than a pure $\ell_1$-norm bias (see Eq. 5 in [1] and Eq. 8 in [2]), as it depends on initialization (e.g., $\alpha_\infty$ in [1] and $R_{a_T}$ in [2]). Although [1] investigated a range of step sizes, it is only up to some small upper bound specified in their Theorem 1. In contrast, we explore a much wider range of step sizes and obtain more general insights. \
Finally, we agree that studying the effects of stochasticity (e.g., SGD noise) and weight decay are interesting avenues for future work and named references provide a good starting point for these. For the sake of comprehensiveness, we have decided to limit our study to the norm and sharpness bias for full-batch GD.

Thanks for pointing out those omitted references on the diagonal model. We have added them in the related works (Appendix A).

**On the chosen sharpness measure**

We restricted ourself to the worst-cased sharpness $S_{\mathcal{L}}$ defined as the operator norm of the loss Hessian. This choice is motivated by theoretical results showing that this version of sharpness is implicitly regularized by gradient descent with large learning rates, see Section 1.3 in our paper.  \
In our literature review we already acknowledge that alternative notions of sharpness have been proposed, including reparametrization-invariant variants. However, reparametrization affects the optimization dynamics, and since our goal is to study the implicit regularization properties of gradient descent itself, it seems natural to us to adopt the theory-grounded definition.

Moreover, given the already comprehensive scope of the paper, we decided to focus on a single, well-justified measure. In response to your comment and to complement our comparison across different norms we have now added an empirical comparison of several sharpness definitions for our two base configurations in the updated Appendix Section H.9. As shown there, other measures of sharpness, including scaling-invariant measures such as adaptive sharpness, display a similar decreasing behavior in the EoS regime and therefore confirm that scaling-invariant measures are also implicitly regularized by GD with large learning rates. This suggests that our claims about a trade-off between sharpness and norm can be extended to other sharpness measures. \
We hope that this also answers your question about the meaning of the sharpness measure when it directly correlates with the learning rate. In case you meant something else, please let us know since we might have misunderstood your question.

Regarding scale invariance, in the plots you refer to (Figures 58 and 59), we have increased the initialization scale. This modification changes the optimization dynamics drastically, as the maximum sharpness along the GF trajectory occurs at initialization. Consequently, the time evolution differs completely: instead of progressive sharpening, the sharpness decreases until it stabilizes around $2/\eta$. 
For the normal initialization scale, the sharpness at initialization allows GF and GD to remain within the standard stability limits, which hints why GF and GD exhibit similar behavior in that regime. Moreover, theoretical results linking GF or GD with small learning rates to $\ell_1$-norm bias typically assume small initialization, so the behavior observed under large-scale initialization lies outside this theoretical setting. We would therefore see the different behaviour in these settings as a showcase of its limitations. We have updated the corresponding Appendix Section H.6 to make this more clear.
 
We hope this clarifies our rationale for choosing the worst-case sharpness measure.

*Please see also part 2 for the continuation of our reply.*

*Part 2 of 2*

**Normalization Layers**

Thanks for raising this interesting connection to the sharpness/norm trade-off with normalization layers. We added this to our discussion in the literature review. We respectfully disagree that this contradicts our observations. In fact, we do not think that the concrete norm value realized by the trained weights determines generalization. We rather believe that the norm-minimizing property influences the relation between single weights in a way that enhances generalization (and this is preserved under re-normalization operations in forward passes). Re-phrased in terms of sparse regression where the underlying ground-truth is assumed to be sparse: For a parameter vector $\beta$ to generalize well, one trains for small $\ell_1$-norm. However, one does so not because a certain $\ell_1$-norm value is important, but because this leads to sparse parameters and thus meaningful relations between the parameter values. 

Note however that, when training with batch normalization and weight decay, we introduce explicit forms of regularization that change the optimization dynamics and induce different biases compared to full-batch gradient descent. In our new experiment where we incorporate batch normalization into the CNN on CIFAR10-5k with CE loss we even still observe a slight U-shaped generalization curve (see Figure 33 in the second revision). Similarly, the trade-off between low sharpness and low parameter norm as we vary the learning rate still remains. We believe that the modified dynamics introduced by normalization represent an interesting direction for further study, but they are beyond the scope of this paper, whose primary goal is to establish a baseline for full-batch gradient descent with a fixed learning rate.

We would like to thank you again for your valuable feedback and would be happy to resolve further concerns or questions.

summary.value: The paper argues that gradient descent’s generalization can’t be explained by a single implicit bias. Instead, the learning rate steers a trade‑off between two biases—small parameter norm and low sharpness (as in Edge‑of‑Stability)—and the best test performance often occurs at intermediate learning rates that balance the two.

strengths.value: The idea of linking norm and sharpness regularization is cool but it is not established in the paper.

weaknesses.value:
The theoretical results are strictly weaker of an already published (more than 1 year ago) and **not cited** paper: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.20531. 

In diagonal linear networks there is no progressive sharpening, when you pick learning rate > 2/\lambda_{\max} of the hessian of the solution at initialization you converge to an oscillatory regime around the min-norm solution, this does not impact the generalization/error of the solution but only the norm of the way the solution is parameterized. It is thus misleading to claim anything about generalization when looking at diagonal linear networks.

Moreover, (as even Cohen et al. (2021), the first paper on EoS, observes) MNIST **does not** show progressive sharpening which is necessary to see the Edge of Stability behavior. In particular, in MNIST the problem is approximately linearly separable. Thus not only no sharpening happens, the opposite! The dynamics will get stabler always exponentially fast (see, e.g., https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.02336).

These are only two of the points that heavily undermine the soundness of any of the claims.

On top of this multiple references are missing, as a blatant example, there is a full line of research existent on the fact that flatness and sharpness do not correlate generally, it started in 2017 with https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.04933, see e.g., https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2023/file/0354767c6386386be17cabe4fc59711b-Paper-Conference.pdf.

On top of it, this is all but a **systematic** experimental analysis! Cifar10 and MNIST is not a systematic experimental analysis in the age of the large models. Even if you are writing a paper about cifar10 and MNIST the argument about generalization is not strong enough for the claims.

I find the contributions are poor and it completely lacks of soundness. Even presentation is too long for no reason and too generic, even in the abstract.

Dear Reviewer F2HG, 

Thank you for your reply. We are glad to hear that all your initial questions have been fully answered.

In response to your review that an evaluation on additional data modalities would be desirable, we have added a new appendix, *H.14 Other Data Modalities*. We have also included the setup of a CNN with batch normalization in *Appendix H.2 Architectures*. These additions are now part of the revised manuscript.

Regarding your new comments: 

As we wrote in response to Reviewer 2XC6, when introducing the risk model, we condition the data distribution to have both coordinates of $x_0$ and $y_0$ positive which makes the solution set an ellipse. Positive features naturally arise when modelling physical quantities.

Furthermore, as you suggested, we now discuss  the “beyond EoS regime” in the literature review in both the main paper and Appendix A. We would like to clarify that, in our understanding, the beyond-EoS regime is characterized by stable oscillation around the (balanced) solution. We would not count such oscillations as convergence, as we only show learning rates where the training loss is below a certain threshold and then stop GD there. Accordingly, such learning rates and the properties of the solutions are excluded in our plots. In addition, we were unable to find the part stating that the balanced minima around which the oscillations occur are of minimal norm, only that they are the flattest ones. Could you please point us to the specific part of the paper? 

We hope that the revision adequately resolves your remaining concerns. If so, we would greatly appreciate it if you would consider updating your score, or let us know if there is anything further we can do to strengthen the manuscript.

summary.value: The paper makes the case that depending on learning rate, GD exhibits different forms of bias (small $\ell_1$-norm for learning rates below a critical threshold value and decreasing sharpness as the learning rate increases beyond the critical threshold). A connection to generalization is drawn with the conclusion that a tradeoff between both biases may be best in some settings. The study is mainly based on extensive experiments, but a very simple model ("shallow diagonal linear network with shared weights") is analyzed theoretically to show that the two types of bias can in fact be very different from each other.

strengths.value: The experiments are relatively comprehensive, covering a range of different settings. The phenomena can be observed consistently throughout (although more cleanly in some experiments than others). The paper is also well presented and easy to read.

weaknesses.value: The paper mostly describes an observed phenomenon and provides some general intuition behind it. However, it was not entirely clear to me what I can do with the result. Is the main message that the learning rate is an important parameter to influence the type of bias? In itself, that does not seem particularly surprising. It has been observed before that GD can behave quite differently from GF. Or it could be the insight that, for generalization, it can be useful to avoid the extreme of either bias and aim for something in between. Maybe it would be interesting to define a new parameterized bias that captures sharpness and $\ell_1$-norm at the extremes and then investigate theoretically how generalization can depend on that parameter?

questions.value: The paper does a very good job of highlighting the different bias behaviors of GD depending on the learning rate, but it could do a better job of pointing out either concrete conclusions/guidance for practitioners and/or open problems that if addressed successfully in future work would have significant impact.

summary.value: This paper investigates the implicit bias of gradient descent under varying step sizes. Through a series of experiments, the authors observed that as the step size increases, the form of the implicit bias transitions from norm regularization to sharpness regularization. In general, the optimal test performance is achieved not at the smallest or largest considered step sizes, but at an intermediate value. The authors thus argued that generalization cannot be explained by a single form of bias. Theoretically, they considered a shallow diagonal linear model with a single data point and showed that the minimum-norm and minimum-sharpness solutions differ, and that neither achieves the lowest generalization error.

strengths.value:
The key message of this paper is that a single form of implicit regularization is not sufficient to explain the generalization. Indeed, much of the existing work on implicit bias has focused on a specific regime of step size (and other hyperparameters), where the bias can be characterized in a relatively clean form. What is less appreciated is how the implicit bias depends on the step size, and which form of the bias is more representative of practical settings. To my knowledge, this aspect has not been much highlighted in the literature, and I therefore find the paper valuable. 

In addition, the paper has several other strengths: 
* The presentation is very clear and the investigation is well motivated. 
* The experiments are well organized and cover a wide range of settings. 
* The phenomena related to the critical step size $\eta_c$ and the phase transition in Figure 1 are particularly interesting.

weaknesses.value:
The theory part of this paper appears relatively weak. As stated in the abstract and Contribution, the goal of the theoretical analyses is to support the main claim of the paper that "*the generalization of neural networks can not be explained by a single implicit bias*". However, I do not think this is achieved by the presented theory, for the following reasons: 

* Results in Section 3 only identified the min-norm and min-sharpness minimizers and showed that they generally differ. This result alone does not support the main claim, as no generalization is concerned. Results concerning generalization, which I believe should be the main part of the theory, are deferred to Appendix E. 

* I find Appendix E also not convincing, as its analysis is confined to a single data point. In the context of *generalization*, I believe a one-sample setting is qualitatively different from realistic settings, and observations made in the former are uninformative for the latter. Specifically, let $w_1$ be the empirical risk minimizer selected by a fixed implicit bias (e.g., norm minimization) and $w_2$ be the empirical risk minimizer that generalizes optimally. The authors aim to argue that $w_1$ and $w_2$ generally differ, hence that generalization can not be explained by a single bias. However, when the sample size is one, the discrepancy between $w_1$ and $w_2$ seems trivial. With a single sample, the empirical risk $L$ is a poor approximation of the population risk $\tilde{L}$. Note $w_1$ solely depends on $L$ whereas $w_2$ strongly depends on $\tilde{L}$. Due to the weak relation between $L$ and $\tilde{L}$, there is no a priori reason to expect that $w_1$​ and $w_2$​ would coincide or even be close. In other words, I think the failure of an implicit bias in a one-sample case merely comes from a lack of data, and does not indicate that this bias is not the "right" explanation for generalization in practice. 



**Initial recommendation**

Despite the above points, I find the main message and the experiments valuable to the community. Therefore, my initial recommendation is borderline acceptance. Nevertheless, I believe revision is needed for acceptance, either to improve the theoretical analyses or to position the work more clearly as an empirical study. In the latter case, I think the paper could still make a valid contribution if the authors are able to provide (even high-level) explanations for the phenomena observed in Figure 1 (see questions below).

questions.value:
I find the presented phenomena, e.g., in Figure 1, very interesting. I understand the following questions may be beyond the paper’s current scope and I do not expect the authors to address each of them in detail. 

* Could the authors comment on the form of the critical step size $\eta_c$? Why is $\eta_c$ related to the maximal sharpness of the GF solutions? This paper [1] might be relevant. 

* The final norm and final sharpness simultaneously exhibit a sharp transition at $\eta=\eta_c$. Could the authors provide intuition for the emergence of such a sharp transition? 

* Could the authors explain the trade off between the final norm and the final sharpness? Why should we expect a decrease in sharpness corresponds to an increase in the norm? This is in contrast with the scalar factorization case, $L(x,y)=(x^\top y - a)^2$, where the squared norm of a minimizer is equal to the sharpness (see, e.g., Theorem F.2., [2]).  

[1] Kreisler, Itai, et al. "Gradient descent monotonically decreases the sharpness of gradient flow solutions in scalar networks and beyond." International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR, 2023.

[2] Yuqing Wang, Minshuo Chen, Tuo Zhao, and Molei Tao. Large Learning Rate Tames Homogeneity: Convergence and Balancing Effect. ICLR 2022

summary.value: The work investigates both theoretically and empirically two competing implicit biases present in deep neural networks. They show that there is a trade-off between norm regularization and sharpness regularization. The empirical part shows that the learning rate controls the trade-off and for good performance a middle ground is required. Theoretically a toy example with one data point is analyzed to illustrate the empirics further.

strengths.value: The framing of the norm and sharpness trade-off furthers the discussion on finding the correct implicit bias trying to explain generalization performance. The paper clearly visualizes the results, making the different biases present easy to understand. Similarly, the toy example explains the competing implicit biases of norm and sharpness minimization. Empirically various factors have been investigated showing a general trend across settings.

weaknesses.value:
The toy example is simplistic, which is also a strength I believe, although for instance in [1] and [2] the effects of SGD noise and weight decay are investigated with more data samples. Based on these two works, would this suggest that the L1 bias is preferred at all times? 
Note that although a continuous model (SDE) is chosen in [1] they do investigate the role of larger learning as well, besides label noise.

The sharpness measure chosen is not scale invariant as can be seen in Fig 58 and 59 and as mentioned in the related work. To isolate the effect of sharpness and scale it could be better to use other sharpness measures as in [3]. What is the meaning of the sharpness measure when it directly will correlate with the learning rate? 
Furthermore, other regularization effects in modern architectures are underexplored such as weight decay and batch norm.
In general, the experiments are of small scale, the results could be strengthened by considering large scale experiments and other data modalities.

Recent works on different aspects of implicit regularization are omitted such as [2, 4, 5, 6] that cover diagonal linear networks.


[1] Pesme, Scott et al. “Implicit Bias of SGD for Diagonal Linear Networks: a Provable Benefit of Stochasticity.” Neural Information Processing Systems (2021).

[2] Jacobs, Tom et al. “Mirror, Mirror of the Flow: How Does Regularization Shape Implicit Bias?” ArXiv abs/2504.12883 (2025): n. pag.

[3] Andriushchenko, Maksym et al. “A modern look at the relationship between sharpness and generalization.” International Conference on Machine Learning (2023).

[4] Wang, Shuyang and Diego Klabjan. “A Mirror Descent Perspective of Smoothed Sign Descent.” Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (2024).

[5] Papazov, Hristo et al. “Leveraging Continuous Time to Understand Momentum When Training Diagonal Linear Networks.” International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics (2024).

[6] Andriushchenko, Maksym and Nicolas Flammarion. “Towards Understanding Sharpness-Aware Minimization.” ArXiv abs/2206.06232 (2022): n. pag.

The novel framing outweighs the limited scope of the experimental and theoretical results, I recommend marginal accept.

Dear Reviewer bSo1,

Upon reading your review carefully, we identified multiple issues, which we detail below. 

> The idea of linking norm and sharpness regularization is cool but it is not established in the paper.

We respectfully disagree. As acknowledged by the other reviewers, we systematically demonstrate in extensive experiments that there is a clear trade-off between low norm and low sharpness of the final learned solution when varying the learning rate and further support this relationship theoretically using a simplified model.

> The theoretical results are strictly weaker of an already published (more than 1 year ago) and not cited paper: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.20531.

While the referenced paper does show an implicit bias of GD with high learning rates towards flat minima, our main contribution is establishing a trade-off between a norm-bias and a sharpness-bias based on varying learning rates. As the paper you mention does not discuss connections to norm-regularization, our results are not included therein. Could you specify in what way our results are strictly weaker? We appreciate the reference suggestion and will include it in our related works discussion in the section on EoS in the next revision.

> In diagonal linear networks there is no progressive sharpening, when you pick learning rate > 2/\lambda_{\max} of the hessian of the solution at initialization you converge to an oscillatory regime around the min-norm solution, this does not impact the generalization/error of the solution but only the norm of the way the solution is parameterized. It is thus misleading to claim anything about generalization when looking at diagonal linear networks.

We do not follow the argument presented in this paragraph. As is standard in most works on EoS, we analyze the dynamics for an initialization with sharpness below $2/\eta$, leading to progressive sharpening during training. It is indeed correct that if the initial learning rate is too large ($> 2/\lambda_{\max}$), GD may fail to converge entirely and does not follow the usual temporal dynamic (progressive sharpening and EoS). However, in the EoS regime, the dynamics typically converge oscillatorily toward solutions of low sharpness, not of low norm, as we systematically demonstrate.

>Moreover, (as even Cohen et al. (2021), the first paper on EoS, observes) MNIST does not show progressive sharpening which is necessary to see the Edge of Stability behavior. In particular, in MNIST the problem is approximately linearly separable. Thus not only no sharpening happens, the opposite! The dynamics will get stabler always exponentially fast (see, e.g., https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.02336).

This is incorrect. First, Cohen et al. do not mention MNIST in their original EoS paper. Second, the paper you mention is also stating that the dynamics at large stepsize are oscillatory, you can see this in the loss curves in Figures 2 and 3. Also shown there is that for too large stepsize (Figure 3), the training diverges. Finally, in our experiments, GD on MNIST indeed does enter progressive sharpening and there are the characteristic EoS oscillations of the sharpness and loss during that phase. We present the temporal evolution of the quantities in Figure 12.

> On top of this multiple references are missing, as a blatant example, there is a full line of research existent on the fact that flatness and sharpness do not correlate generally, it started in 2017 with https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.04933, see e.g., https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2023/file/0354767c6386386be17cabe4fc59711b-Paper-Conference.pdf.

We emphasize that we **do** cite both of the mentioned references, and discuss them in our literature review (see lines 242 and 923 of the original submission). If you believe any relevant work is missing, we would be happy if you can point it out to us, but please first check the list of references of our paper to avoid further confusion.

> On top of it, this is all but a systematic experimental analysis! Cifar10 and MNIST is not a systematic experimental analysis in the age of the large models. [...]

We respectfully disagree. Our study systematically varies core components of the training, namely dataset size, architecture (both width/depth and model class), activation function, loss function, loss threshold, initialization and parametrization. While we agree that MNIST and CIFAR10 are not state-of-the-art image data sets, we chose them to have a complementing difficulty level while keeping the computational cost, in particular the sharpness computation, feasible.

> [...] Even presentation is too long for no reason and too generic, even in the abstract.

Three of the other reviewers have rated the presentation as good to excellent. If you have any specific suggestion for improving our presentation, we would be happy to hear it. 

We would be happy to provide further clarifications. Nevertheless, we would appreciate a constructive discussion.
